title: Could Large Hadron Collider Operations Produce Catastrophic Microscopic Black Holes? (2008 Public Dispute)
summary: In 2008, ahead of LHC startup, public concern arose that proton-proton collisions might create microscopic black holes capable of growing and destroying Earth. The CERN-commissioned LHC Safety Assessment Group (LSAG) and the underlying Giddings-Mangano analysis argued that Hawking evaporation, and independently the survival of cosmic-ray-bombarded white dwarfs and neutron stars, rule out any danger. A dissenting preprint by R. Plaga argued that a microcanonical treatment of black hole thermodynamics could leave Hawking radiation strongly suppressed but not eliminated, permitting metastable, Eddington-accreting black holes that would evade the safety bounds; Giddings and Mangano rebutted this directly, and later independent work (Koch, Bleicher & Stoecker; Casadio, Fabi & Harms) offered additional arguments against catastrophic growth, though the latter also conceded longer-than-typical decay times within its model. This case includes normalized claims, a relation graph capturing agreement and dispute among the sources, and an assessment layer identifying cruxes, failure modes, and missing evidence bearing on the dispute; all content remains marked as unverified against primary sources pending manual review.

extracted_claims.raw_text: Any microscopic black holes produced at the LHC are expected to decay by Hawking radiation before they reach the detector walls.
If some microscopic black holes were stable, those produced by cosmic rays would be stopped inside the Earth or other astronomical bodies.
The stability of astronomical bodies constrains strongly the possible rate of accretion by any such microscopic black holes, so that they present no conceivable danger.

There is... one significant difference between cosmic-ray collisions with a body at rest and collisions at the LHC, namely that any massive new particles produced by the LHC collisions will tend to have low velocities, whereas cosmic-ray collisions would produce them with high velocities.
This point has been considered in detail [2] since the 2003 report by the LHC Safety Study Group [1].
As we now discuss, the original conclusion that LHC collisions present no dangers is validated and strengthened by this more recent work.
There is broad consensus among physicists on the reality of Hawking radiation, but so far no experiment has had the sensitivity required to find direct evidence for it.

Independently of the reasoning based on Hawking radiation, if microscopic black holes were to be singly produced by colliding the quarks and gluons inside protons, they would also be able to decay into the same types of particles that produced them.

The reason being that in this case they could not carry any conserved quantum number that is not already carried by the original quarks and gluons, and their decay back to the initial state partons would be allowed.
For this reason, a microscopic black hole cannot be completely black.
In fact, ultra-high-energy cosmic rays hitting dense stars such as white dwarfs and neutron stars would have produced black holes copiously during their lifetimes.
Such black holes, even if neutral, would have been stopped by the material inside such dense stars.

The rapid accretion due to the large density of these bodies, and to the strong gravitational interactions of these black holes, would have led to the destruction of white dwarfs and neutron stars on time scales that are much shorter than their observed lifetimes.
The final stages of their destruction would have released explosively large amounts of energy, that would have been highly visible.
The observation of white dwarfs and neutron stars that would have been destroyed in this way tells us that cosmic rays do not produce such black holes, and hence neither will the LHC.

We analyze macroscopic effects of TeV-scale black holes, such as could possibly be produced at the LHC, in what is regarded as an extremely hypothetical scenario in which they are stable and, if trapped inside Earth, begin to accrete matter.
We examine a wide variety of TeV-scale gravity scenarios, basing the resulting accretion models on first-principles, basic, and well-tested physical laws.
These scenarios fall into two classes, depending on whether accretion could have any macroscopic effect on the Earth at times shorter than the Sun's natural lifetime.

We argue that cases with such effect at shorter times than the solar lifetime are ruled out, since in these scenarios black holes produced by cosmic rays impinging on much denser white dwarfs and neutron stars would then catalyze their decay on timescales incompatible with their known lifetimes.
In order for our bounds to have relevance, a sequence of unlikely things would have to be true.

First, TeV scale gravity, with a Planck scale no higher than a few TeV, would have to be correct, so that black holes can be produced at LHC. Most workers consider this to be a fascinating possibility, but also a somewhat unlikely possibility.

Second, black hole radiance, which has been deeply studied from a number of theoretical perspectives, would have to be wrong, and more general quantum mechanical arguments for black hole instability would have to be wrong. Most workers consider this to be an exceedingly improbable, if not impossible, scenario.

Finally, one would need a mechanism to shut off the quantum effects responsible for Hawking radiation, but still leave intact either the quantum effects responsible for Schwinger discharge, or some other neutralization mechanism that acts to discharge the resulting stable black holes. It is very difficult to conceive of a consistent physical framework that provides such a mechanism.

Moreover, decay of observed neutron stars would also have been catalyzed, unless both of two unlikely possibilities are realized, namely that the composition of ultrahigh-energy cosmic ray primaries is dominantly heavy elements, and ultrahigh energy cosmic ray neutrinos either are not produced, or have suppressed gravitational interactions with partons.

The question of whether collider produced of subnuclear black holes might constitute a catastrophic risk is explored in a model of Casadio & Harms (2002) that treats them as quantum-mechanical objects.

extracted_claims.raw_text: Where did [1] go wrong? The answer is in the inconsistent application of formula (2) of that paper.

In the type of warped scenario that [1] considers, the black hole would evolve up to a radius R ∼ R_D via higher-dimensional evolution, and then would experience a large mass gain in transitioning to a slightly higher radius R ∼ R_C, as [1] acknowledges.

Throughout this region, in the usual Hawking scenario, the temperature formula (2) should hold. Thus if the black hole radiance is suppressed compared to this, as the author of [1] proposes, it can't exceed a value of size (3).

However, [1] then applies the formula (1) written in terms of the mass using the four-dimensional relationship between radius and mass, but does this in a region where the four-dimensional relation between radius and mass is clearly wrong.

extracted_claims.raw_text: First, in such a "suppressed Hawking radiation" scenario, the arguments of [2] tell us that one can in fact not establish Eddington-limited accretion in a white dwarf (see in particular eq.(B.13) in [2]); so, even ignoring the inconsistency we reported above, the bounds of that paper would apply even to the suggested scenario of [1].

extracted_claims.raw_text: There is to our knowledge no scientific work that predicts that the remnants (if they exist) of such mini black holes (if they exist) could be stable at masses far above the Planck scale M_f.

However, given the public alarm over the subject, we want to go further and also exclude danger from scenarios which are to the present understanding of the physics of mini black holes not well motivated.

A number of counter arguments disfavor such disaster scenarios. Recently those arguments have been summarized and discussed by a group [15] who comes to the conclusion that "there is no risk of any significance whatsoever from such black holes".
extracted_claims.extraction_notes: excerpt lhc_c014; embedded quotation is Koch et al. quoting Giddings-Mangano (src_002/ref [15]).

extracted_claims.raw_text: In this paper we independently present a short coherent argument why there is no risk due to mini black holes from TeV particle collisions. First we look at the logically possible black hole evolution paths. After this we show for every endpoint of the paths, why mini black holes can not be dangerously growing.

For this we use arguments which are already present in [15], but we also bring forward new arguments such as the influence of a strongly growing black hole mass on the escape velocity of the mini black hole.
In order for the black holes created at the LHC to grow at all, the critical mass should be M_c ≳ 10² kg.
This value is already larger than the maximum compatible with experimental tests of Newton's law (and we further relaxed it to M_c = 10⁴ kg in our analysis).
For smaller values of M_c, the black holes cannot accrete fast enough to overcome the decay rate.
We conclude that, for the RS scenario and black holes described by the metric (6), the growth of black holes to catastrophic size is not possible.

Casadio, Fabi & Harms's conclusion of no catastrophic growth in the RS scenario (NC_021) rests on the critical-mass bound established in NC_020 (lhc_c015, lhc_c016).

Per the packet's framing, Casadio-Fabi-Harms work within the scenario closest to Plaga's own assumptions (the microcanonical framework's originators) and still conclude catastrophic growth is not possible, undercutting the viability of Plaga's harmful scenario (NC_011).

NC_009 originates in src_009 (Plaga); the src_012 excerpt (lhc_c016) cites 'Ref. [4]', most plausibly Casadio & Harms's own earlier work, not Plaga's paper specifically. Reclassified per AF_003: the link between NC_021's decay-time concession and NC_009's suppressed-radiation premise is an analyst-drawn cross-source inference, not something either source excerpt states directly.

The harmful accretion/emission scenario in NC_011 is only meaningful if the suppressed-but-nonzero radiation premise of NC_009 holds; this dependency is not stated outright but follows from the structure of Plaga's argument.

cruxes.statement: Does the kinematic difference between LHC collisions (low-velocity products in the lab frame) and cosmic-ray collisions (high-velocity products) undermine the validity of using cosmic-ray/astronomical-body survival as a safety proxy for LHC-produced black holes?
cruxes.description: The entire cosmic-ray-based safety argument (NC_006) assumes that black holes produced by cosmic rays hitting astronomical bodies are a valid stand-in for black holes produced at the LHC. LSAG concedes a genuine velocity difference exists but asserts (citing Giddings-Mangano) that detailed analysis 'validates and strengthens' rather than undermines the argument. If this kinematic disanalogy were shown to matter, the central astrophysical safety bound would need re-derivation; if not, it remains solid support for NC_006.
cruxes.resolution_notes: No source in this packet independently (i.e., outside the Giddings-Mangano/LSAG lineage) re-derives or contests the velocity-difference analysis; it is asserted as settled by the same interconnected author group that produced both the technical paper and the review that cites it.

cruxes.statement: Is Hawking radiation (or an equivalent complete-evaporation mechanism) real and total enough to guarantee that LHC-produced microscopic black holes decay before causing harm, or could a microcanonical (fixed-energy) treatment yield only strongly suppressed, non-zero radiation permitting metastable, potentially hazardous black holes?
cruxes.description: This is the deepest technical fork in the dispute. NC_001/NC_003 rely on (or independently argue around) Hawking decay; NC_002 concedes no direct experimental confirmation of Hawking radiation exists; NC_009/NC_010/NC_011 (Plaga) argue a microcanonical treatment yields only strong suppression, not shutoff. If Hawking radiation is confirmed complete, the con position is strongly vindicated; if suppression at small mass is real and significant, Plaga's metastable-black-hole risk scenario becomes more credible.
cruxes.resolution_notes: No direct experimental test of Hawking radiation existed as of the packet's sources (2008-2009), and the microcanonical-vs-canonical ensemble question is a live theoretical dispute, not an empirically settled one within this packet.

cruxes.statement: Is Koch, Bleicher & Stoecker's enumeration of logically possible black-hole evolution endpoints actually exhaustive, such that no additional physically plausible dangerous pathway has been omitted?
cruxes.description: NC_019's argument-by-exhaustion safety conclusion is only as strong as the completeness of its enumerated evolution paths. Plaga's completeness objection (NC_013) directly challenges this for the related Giddings-Mangano and Koch analyses, alleging exclusion of plausible parameter ranges without justification. If the enumeration is genuinely exhaustive, NC_019 stands as strong independent corroboration of safety; if not, an unconsidered pathway could reopen the risk question.
cruxes.resolution_notes: No formal completeness proof is presented in the packet; the enumeration's exhaustiveness is asserted, not demonstrated, and is directly disputed (in general terms) by Plaga.

cruxes.statement: Do the astrophysical (white-dwarf/neutron-star) accretion-timescale bounds derived by Giddings & Mangano actually constrain all physically plausible black-hole scenarios -- including Plaga's suppressed-radiation, Eddington-limited-accretion scenario -- or can some parameter ranges evade these bounds?
cruxes.description: This is the central point of direct confrontation in the dispute. Giddings & Mangano (src_010) argue their bounds apply even to Plaga's scenario via their eq. B.13 (NC_016); Plaga claims his scenario evades exactly these exclusions (NC_012) and that the analyses are incomplete (NC_013). Casadio-Fabi-Harms (working in the framework closest to Plaga's own assumptions) independently find catastrophic growth impossible in the RS scenario (NC_020/NC_021), which weighs against Plaga's evasion claim but is itself model-specific.
cruxes.resolution_notes: No third-party (non-author) adjudication of this specific technical disagreement appears in the packet; Casadio-Fabi-Harms's independent result is supportive but model-specific (RS scenario only) and does not directly address Plaga's Eddington-limit mechanism.

cruxes.statement: Was there a genuine technical/mathematical error in Plaga's application of the four-dimensional mass-radius relation (as alleged by Giddings & Mangano in src_010), or is the disagreement purely a matter of differing initial assumptions about black-hole properties, as Plaga himself claims?
cruxes.description: Plaga (NC_014) frames the dispute as assumption-level, implying no technical fault in either side's calculations. Giddings & Mangano (NC_015) directly contest this, alleging Plaga misapplies a formula outside its valid regime. Because this exchange occurred entirely via non-peer-reviewed arXiv notes with no independent referee or third-party theorist weighing in, the equation-level dispute has never been formally adjudicated.
cruxes.resolution_notes: Both sides' claims here come from non-peer-reviewed sources with strong incentive alignment (each defending their own analysis); no independent verification exists in the packet.

failure_mode_flags.description: LSAG (src_001) is a CERN-commissioned review of the safety of CERN's own flagship experiment; the institution being reviewed and the institution commissioning the review are the same, creating a structural incentive to reach a reassuring conclusion regardless of the underlying evidentiary strength.
failure_mode_flags.notes: The technical content is peer-reviewed and partially corroborated by non-CERN authors (Koch et al.), which mitigates but does not eliminate the incentive concern.

failure_mode_flags.description: Mangano is co-author of both the central technical safety analysis (src_002) and the official LSAG review (src_001) that cites and endorses it, reducing the independence of the two-source 'corroboration' that the safety case relies on.
failure_mode_flags.notes: src_002 is peer-reviewed in Physical Review D, which offsets some of this concern, but does not resolve the shared-authorship dependency with src_001.

failure_mode_flags.description: src_010 is a rebuttal note written by the same authors (Giddings & Mangano) whose earlier work (src_002) is being defended against Plaga's criticism; it is not an independent adjudication and was never peer-reviewed or journal-published.
failure_mode_flags.notes: Applied symmetrically alongside FF_002 to flag non-independence on the 'con' (safety) side of the dispute, mirroring FF_004 on the 'pro' (risk) side.

failure_mode_flags.description: Plaga (src_009), as sole author advancing a dissenting catastrophic-risk hypothesis in a non-peer-reviewed preprint, has a reputational incentive to establish that a previously overlooked risk exists; this is the mirror-image incentive concern to FF_001-FF_003 on the safety side.
failure_mode_flags.notes: Applied to maintain symmetry: incentive-pressure concerns are not unique to institution-affiliated 'safety' sources.

failure_mode_flags.description: R_006 treats the detailed kinematic (velocity-difference) analysis as an independent strengthening of the safety conclusion, but the 'more recent work' referenced is the Giddings-Mangano paper (src_002), authored in part by the same person (Mangano) who co-authors the LSAG review citing it -- this is not independent corroboration.

R_021 frames Koch et al.'s argument as 'independent corroboration' of Giddings-Mangano's no-danger conclusion, but Koch et al. explicitly quote and build from Giddings-Mangano's conclusion and share the same disciplinary community (collider phenomenology), somewhat limiting true independence even though authorship is distinct.
failure_mode_flags.notes: Less severe than FF_005 since Koch et al. are a genuinely distinct author group and add a novel argument (escape velocity).

failure_mode_flags.description: The expectation that LHC-produced microscopic black holes decay via Hawking radiation before reaching detector walls (NC_001) rests entirely on theoretical prediction; Hawking radiation itself has never been directly experimentally observed (as conceded in NC_002).
failure_mode_flags.notes: Central to CX_002; mitigated somewhat by the independent back-decay argument in NC_003, which does not rely on Hawking radiation.

failure_mode_flags.description: Plaga's central harmful-scenario claim (NC_011) -- that metastable black holes would accrete at the Eddington limit and emit harmful radiation -- is a purely theoretical extrapolation from a contested thermodynamic framework; there is no direct observational or experimental evidence of any such accretion event.
failure_mode_flags.notes: Applied symmetrically alongside FF_007 to flag the same failure mode on the 'pro-risk' side of the dispute. Severity aligned with FF_007 (significant) since no independent justification was found for weighting the identical evidentiary gap more heavily against the dissenting position (see AF_005).

failure_mode_flags.description: The astrophysical safety argument (NC_006) depends on treating cosmic-ray-induced black-hole production in astronomical bodies as analogous to LHC-collision-induced production, despite an acknowledged kinematic (velocity) disanalogy that requires a separate supporting argument (NC_008) to bridge.
failure_mode_flags.notes: Directly relevant to CX_001; the bridging argument (NC_008) is asserted by the same non-independent author lineage flagged in FF_005.

failure_mode_flags.description: Plaga's suppressed-Hawking-radiation premise (NC_009) assumes the microcanonical (fixed total energy) ensemble is the physically correct description of small-mass quantum black-hole thermodynamics rather than the canonical ensemble used by Giddings-Mangano; this foundational choice is asserted (NC_010) rather than independently established.
failure_mode_flags.notes: Directly relevant to CX_002; applied symmetrically alongside FF_011 which flags a hidden assumption on the safety side.

failure_mode_flags.description: The back-decay argument (NC_003) assumes single-parton-channel production dominates and that no additional conserved quantum numbers beyond those already carried by initial partons exist; both are physically reasonable but unstated background assumptions rather than independently verified facts.
failure_mode_flags.notes: Lower severity than FF_010 because this argument is widely accepted in the particle-physics community and less contested than the microcanonical ensemble question.

failure_mode_flags.description: LSAG's phrase that stable black holes 'present no conceivable danger' (embedded in NC_006) is a strong, unqualified-sounding conclusion that overstates the underlying argument, which is in fact a long conditional chain (see NC_004, NC_007 caveats) rather than an unconditional result.
failure_mode_flags.notes: The rhetorical force of 'no conceivable danger' and 'no risk of any significance whatsoever from such black holes' (echoed in NC_019) exceeds what the hedged, multi-conditional technical argument actually establishes.

failure_mode_flags.description: NC_002 asserts 'broad consensus among physicists' that Hawking radiation is real without specifying what that consensus depends on (e.g., semiclassical quantum-field-theory-in-curved-spacetime assumptions, validity at trans-Planckian scales), making it hard to assess how new theoretical developments (e.g., microcanonical treatments) should update that consensus.
failure_mode_flags.notes: Relevant to CX_002; the consensus claim is plausible but under-specified in the source excerpt itself.

failure_mode_flags.description: Plaga's claim that his proposed metastable black holes 'remain undetectable in existing astrophysical observations' (NC_012) does not specify the observational threshold, parameter space, or detection method against which undetectability is being assessed, making the 'evasion' claim difficult to evaluate precisely.
failure_mode_flags.notes: Applied on the 'pro-risk' side to maintain symmetry with vagueness-adjacent rhetorical concerns flagged on the safety side (FF_012).

failure_mode_flags.description: Koch, Bleicher & Stoecker (src_011) are collider phenomenologists within the same research community as Giddings & Mangano, as the source's own limitations note states; while methodologically distinct and independently authored, they share disciplinary incentives (favorable reception within the collider-physics community) to reach a reassuring conclusion, a concern not previously flagged for this source.
failure_mode_flags.notes: Added to correct asymmetric flagging noted in AF_004: incentive-pressure concerns had been applied to src_001, src_002, src_009, src_010 but not to src_011.

failure_mode_flags.description: Casadio, Fabi & Harms (src_012) are the originators of the microcanonical thermodynamic framework that Plaga's dissenting risk argument (NC_009) relies on; their own paper concluding that catastrophic growth is not possible within that same framework carries a plausible reputational incentive to show their framework does not entail the risk Plaga derives from it.
failure_mode_flags.notes: Added to correct asymmetric flagging noted in AF_004: no source_incentive_pressure flag had previously been applied to src_012 despite a plausible motive.

missing_evidence.description: Direct experimental detection of gravitational Hawking radiation from any black hole (as opposed to indirect analog-gravity demonstrations) does not exist. This would directly test the core mechanism NC_001 relies on and would help adjudicate the microcanonical-vs-canonical dispute (CX_002).
missing_evidence.reason_absent: Predicted Hawking temperatures for astrophysical black holes are far below the cosmic microwave background, making direct astrophysical detection currently infeasible; laboratory/analog-gravity experiments (e.g., sonic black holes) provide suggestive but not equivalent evidence.

missing_evidence.description: No independent, third-party (i.e., not authored by Giddings, Mangano, or Plaga) peer-reviewed adjudication of the specific technical dispute over whether Plaga misapplied the four-dimensional mass-radius relation exists. This would resolve CX_005.
missing_evidence.reason_absent: The exchange occurred entirely through arXiv notes/preprints (src_009, src_010) without formal journal peer review or a published third-party analysis engaging the specific equations.

missing_evidence.description: Precise observational data on ultra-high-energy cosmic-ray primary composition (light vs. heavy elements) and on UHE cosmic-ray neutrino production/interaction rates at the relevant energies does not yet exist at sufficient statistical power. This directly bears on the neutron-star-leg caveat (NC_004) and thus CX_004.
missing_evidence.reason_absent: Statistics at the required ultra-high energies remain limited even with current cosmic-ray observatories.

missing_evidence.description: A formal, rigorous proof (rather than an informal enumeration) that Koch, Bleicher & Stoecker's set of black-hole evolution endpoints is exhaustive does not exist. This would resolve CX_003.
missing_evidence.reason_absent: Not yet undertaken; the original paper enumerates paths informally/heuristically rather than via a formal classification argument.

missing_evidence.description: Post-2009 empirical results from over a decade of actual LHC operation (searches for TeV-scale gravity signatures, missing-energy anomalies, and any microscopic-black-hole-like events) are absent from this source packet, which is frozen at 2008-2009 sources. Such data would bear directly on precondition (1) of NC_007 (whether TeV-scale gravity with a Planck scale of a few TeV is correct) and thus on CX_002 as a whole.
missing_evidence.reason_absent: This packet's source list was assembled from 2008-2009 documents only; later ATLAS/CMS search results and broader post-2010 literature were not ingested into this case.

assessments.perspective: primary builder, synthesizing the 2008-2009 source packet as given
assessments.summary: Within the 2008-2009 source record, the dominant scientific position (LSAG, Giddings-Mangano, Koch et al.) that LHC-produced microscopic black holes pose no meaningful catastrophic risk is well-argued and multiply corroborated in structure, but the corroborating sources are not fully independent of one another, and the central theoretical mechanisms (Hawking radiation) and the principal dissenting technical objection (Plaga's suppressed-radiation scenario) were not fully and independently adjudicated within the packet. The dispute is best characterized as practically resolved by scientific consensus and subsequent safe operation, but not fully settled at the level of first-principles theoretical adjudication captured in these sources.
assessments.settled_direction: The preponderance of theoretical analysis available in this packet, reinforced by the largely independent Koch et al. and Casadio-Fabi-Harms papers, supports the conclusion that catastrophic LHC black-hole risk is negligible to the point of practical non-concern. This is 'settled' as a matter of mainstream physics assessment, but the underlying cruxes (whether Hawking radiation is total, whether the astrophysical bounds cover all suppressed-radiation parameter space, and whether Plaga's specific technical error claim is correct) remain formally unresolved within the evidence in this packet.
assessments.epistemic_status_summary: Multiple independent-ish theoretical analyses converge on 'no meaningful risk,' but convergence is partly an artifact of shared authorship (Mangano appears in both the technical paper and the official review) and shared disciplinary background (all safety-side authors are collider phenomenologists). The sole dissenting voice (Plaga) is a single non-peer-reviewed preprint whose central mechanism is directly disputed by a non-peer-reviewed rebuttal from the authors it criticizes -- neither side of that specific technical exchange was independently adjudicated in a journal.
assessments.confidence: medium-high that the practical conclusion (no catastrophic risk) is correct, given real-world operational history; lower confidence that every specific theoretical crux in this packet was fully and independently resolved.

sensitivity.effect_if_overturned: If Hawking radiation were shown to be strongly suppressed at small masses (vindicating the microcanonical framework), the con position's central mechanism (NC_001) would weaken substantially, though the independent back-decay argument (NC_003) and astrophysical bounds (NC_006, contingent on CX_004) could still provide separate safety grounds.

If the astrophysical bounds were shown not to cover Plaga's suppressed-radiation/Eddington-accretion parameter space, the safety case would lose its principal fallback argument and would need to rely more heavily on the (also contested) claim of a calculational error in Plaga's work (CX_005).

Even if the astrophysical white-dwarf/neutron-star argument were undermined for the neutron-star leg specifically (per NC_004's caveat), the white-dwarf leg and independent Koch et al./Casadio et al. arguments would still provide some support for the overall safety conclusion, though with reduced strength.

Even if Plaga's specific Eddington-limit mechanism were fully vindicated, Giddings-Mangano's fallback argument (NC_016) and Casadio-Fabi-Harms's independent critical-mass bound (NC_020/NC_021, derived within the framework closest to Plaga's own assumptions) would still constrain the practical magnitude of any resulting risk.

what_would_update.scenario: Direct experimental or astrophysical confirmation (or disconfirmation) of gravitational Hawking radiation as a complete evaporation mechanism.
An independent, peer-reviewed, third-party adjudication of the Plaga/Giddings-Mangano technical dispute over the four-dimensional mass-radius relation, confirming one side's claim over the other.
New observational data resolving the composition of ultra-high-energy cosmic-ray primaries and the production/interaction rates of UHE cosmic-ray neutrinos.
Incorporation into this case of post-2009 LHC operational data (searches for TeV-scale gravity / microscopic-black-hole signatures) showing no evidence for low-scale quantum gravity.
Discovery of any observed instance of stable or metastable microscopic-black-hole accretion behavior, at the LHC or in astrophysical data.

assessments.notes: This assessment treats 'catastrophic harm' framing as the operative risk question per the case title; it does not independently verify any primary source and should be read as a structural analysis of the packet as assembled, not as a physics adjudication.
